lead: Rapid prototyping makes a physical model from a CAD design quickly, so a designer can hold a part, check its shape, fit and function, and correct errors before costly tooling. The model is not machined or cast from a drawing; it is built layer by layer from a digital file. The fixed route goes from CAD solid to STL mesh, build orientation, supports, sliced layers, layer build and post-processing. Industry uses it for new product checks, custom medical guides, pump housings and consumer product prototypes.
prereq: You need Chapter 7.1 and basic CAD drawing.

blocks.text: Market pressure pushes a product through many design changes before a production line is ordered. A drawing or screen view hides clashes, weak corners and awkward assembly. A rapid prototype is a physical model made directly from the CAD data, usually in hours or a few days, so the team can check three things: form (does it look and measure right), fit (does it mate with the next part), and function (does it work in a simple test).

Early AM was used mainly for such models, hence the name rapid prototyping. The same chain now makes tooling inserts and end-use parts, covered in Chapter 7.9. The value is shorter design iteration: one physical check can expose an error that several drawings miss.

A Chennai appliance maker may print a fan housing to test airflow and screw bosses before cutting a mould. If a boss is 2 mm too short, the change is made in CAD and a new model is printed; no mould is scrapped. The prototype need not use final material. It must answer the question asked of it: shape, fit, or a short functional trial.
The generic chain converts a CAD solid into machine instructions and then a part. Some syllabi call this the AM process chain.

items: CAD model: a closed solid or a well-defined surface model, saved in the design unit, usually millimetres.
STL file: the surface is approximated by triangles; each triangle has three vertices and a normal that gives its facing direction.
Orient and support: choose the build direction, place supports under overhangs (faces that lean over empty space) and decide the build plate position.
Slice: the software cuts the supported model into thin horizontal layers and creates tool paths.
Build: the machine adds material layer by layer; the path depends on the process.
Post-process: remove the part, take off supports, clean, cure, machine or paint as needed.

blocks.text: The order is fixed because each step depends on the previous one. Slicing cannot start until orientation and supports are fixed; the machine cannot build until slices exist. The build direction also decides which faces need support and which faces touch the build plate. The layer-building physics belongs to Chapter 7.3 onwards.

STL is a surface triangle mesh, not a solid model of tiny volume cells. A flat face may need two triangles; a curved face may need hundreds. More triangles give a smoother curve but a larger file. Common STL errors are holes, flipped normals, zero-area triangles and several disconnected shells. The file has no units; the designer and the machine operator must agree whether 1 means 1 mm or 1 inch. A 40 mm part exported in inches can arrive as about 1016 mm.

Build orientation changes build time, support volume and surface finish. A tall thin part may need many supports; laid flat it may need fewer supports but a poorer face on the build plate side. Round holes may become slightly oval if the layer plane cuts them at an angle.

blocks.where: N is the number of layers; H is the part height in mm along the build direction; t is the layer thickness in mm. Both H and t must use the same unit.

blocks.text: Thin layers, say 0.1 mm, give a smoother curved surface and finer detail but double the layer count compared with 0.2 mm. More layers mean longer build time and more chances for a small error. Thick layers are faster but show visible stair steps on sloping faces.

examples.question: A cylindrical test model is 40 mm tall. It is sliced at a layer thickness of 0.2 mm. (a) Find the number of layers. (b) The designer changes the layer thickness to 0.1 mm. Find the new number of layers.
steps: Height H = 40 mm. First layer thickness t₁ = 0.2 mm.
Use N = H ÷ t. N₁ = 40 mm ÷ 0.2 mm = 200. The unit mm cancels.
Check: halving the layer thickness doubles the layer count: 200 × 2 = 400.
examples.answer: At 0.2 mm the model has 200 layers; at 0.1 mm it has 400 layers.
examples.check:
height_mm = 40
thickness_1 = 0.2
thickness_2 = 0.1
layers_1 = height_mm / thickness_1
layers_2 = height_mm / thickness_2
print(int(layers_1))
print(int(layers_2))

traps: STL is a surface triangle mesh, not a solid model of tiny volume cells. Do not say STL stores material inside the part.
Layer count is height ÷ layer thickness, not volume ÷ layer volume. Mixing the two gives a meaningless number.
Halving layer thickness doubles layer count for the same height; it does not halve build time.
Build orientation is chosen before slicing. A support-free orientation may still be rejected because a critical face becomes rough.
Removing supports and post-curing are part of the AM chain; the part is not finished when the machine stops.

quiz.q: What does an STL file store?
quiz.a: A surface mesh of triangles with vertices and normals; it does not store a solid volume.

quiz.q: Why is a physical prototype useful even when a full 3D CAD view exists?
quiz.a: It reveals form, fit and function issues that a screen image can hide, such as clashes, feel, assembly and simple working tests.

quiz.q: A part is 25 mm tall and sliced at 0.25 mm. Find the number of layers.
A designer rotates a part to reduce supports, but a visible face becomes rough. Explain the trade-off.
quiz.a: Orientation changes support volume and surface finish; reducing supports can put a critical face on a rough support side or build-plate side, so the choice must protect the functional face.

quiz.q: Name the steps of the generic AM chain in order.
quiz.a: CAD model, STL, orient and support, slice, build, post-process, finished part.

quiz.q: Why must units be agreed before STL export?
quiz.a: STL carries no units; a 40 mm dimension can be read as 40 inches, making the part about 25 times too large.

quiz.q: A 60 mm tall part is built at 0.15 mm. If layer thickness rises to 0.3 mm, find old and new layer counts and state one effect on surface finish.
quiz.a: N₁ = 60 ÷ 0.15 = 400; N₂ = 60 ÷ 0.3 = 200; thicker layers are faster but show larger stair steps.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production teams now use cloud slicing and simulation to choose orientation before printing, and file formats such as 3MF carry units, colour and material data that STL cannot. Designers search for design for additive manufacturing (DFAM), support minimisation and build-time estimation. The same chain appears in bioprinting and construction printing, where the layer is a bead of material rather than a thin slice. Search terms: STL repair, 3MF, build orientation optimisation, DFAM.
